Specifically, in the energy ranges above 4 to 8 EeV and above 8 EeV, a notable dipolar modulation in right ascension was observed. Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 36GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a decision feedback equalizer was initially applied with satisfactory results, however its effectiveness was impeded due to the occurrence of burst errors resulting from unpredictable marine conditions. To mitigate this issue, a weighted DFE method was developed but proved insufficient as it was unable to fully compensate for the spectral distortions due to the limited scope of its feedback symbols. To address these limitations, the introduction of maximum likelihood sequence estimation after WDFE proved capable of both rectifying the spectral distortions and providing optimal detection, ultimately yielding a maximum 2.9dB enhancement in signal quality and eliminating BER floors, thereby providing a viable solution for mitigating the detrimental effects of burst errors in fiber-optic communications systems.

Networks (TCNs) have shown great promise for handling time-series data. However, optimizing the time-dilated convolution aspect of TCNs requires a considerable amount of experimentation. We've developed an automatic optimizer that tackles this challenge by treating dilation factor selection as a weight pruning problem on the time-axis. This method learns dilation factors alongside model weights during training, leading to significant reductions in model size and inference latency on real hardware by up to 7.4x and 3x respectively, without compromising accuracy. Furthermore, it enables the discovery of multiple optimal TCN configurations from a single model, outperforming hand-crafted solutions in both efficiency and accuracy.

massive arc-like structure on the sky at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 gigaparsec in size, this structure, known as the Giant Arc, appears almost symmetrical on the sky and was discovered through the presence of magnesium II absorbers in the spectra of background quasars. Utilizing magnesium II absorbers offers a novel approach to investigating large-scale structures at redshifts between 0.45 and 1.35. We present the observational characteristics of the Giant Arc and evaluate its statistical significance using three distinct methods: hierarchical clustering, the Cuzick-Edwards test, and power spectrum analysis. Each of these approaches has unique attributes and provides compelling evidence when considered collectively. To address potential biases in our analysis, we employed strategies to mitigate post-discovery significance assessments. The Giant Arc exhibits an overdensity of approximately 1.3, with a margin of error of 0.3. This structure is part of a growing collection of massive large-scale structures that may challenge the cosmological principle, which underlies the standard model of cosmology. The Giant Arc could be a precursor to a structure like the Sloan Great Wall, but on a much larger scale, observed when the universe was half its current age.

using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention. Two primary approaches, direct methods and two-stage pipelines, can be distinguished based on whether intermediate cues are employed. In the latter category, CNNs first regress intermediate cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points in the initial stage. These intermediate cues then facilitate the computation of object pose through constructed correspondence constraints. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by integrating two distinct concepts: projection grouping and correspondence learning. We begin by utilizing a local patch-based method to generate projection heatmaps, representing the confidence distribution of projected 3D bounding box corners. A projection grouping module is then introduced to combine adjacent heatmaps, eliminating redundant components and producing a compact representation of projection clusters. Consequently, the correspondence learning module is designed to establish correspondence relationships between projection clusters and 2D object candidate instances, rather than relying on exhaustive search. Experimental evaluations on three public datasets demonstrate the superiority of the proposed framework over existing state-of-the-art methods.

Bond-Based Peridynamics, despite its limitations, has become a widely used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation, physical coherence, and stability. This paper reviews and examines various aspects of bond-based peridynamic models, providing a detailed overview of the peridynamics theory, its applications, and numerical models. The employed BB-PD integral kernels are discussed, highlighting their differences and commonalities, as well as the implications of their mathematical structure. A critical analysis is also presented of the role of nonlocality in kinematics, the relationship between kernel structure and material impenetrability, and the influence of PD kernel nonlinearity on crack formation prediction. Finally, the idea of extending BB-PD to fluid dynamics is proposed and explored within the framework of fading memory materials, offering potential perspectives for a deeper understanding of peridynamics in fluid systems.

This library builds upon the Graphical Lasso method, initially introduced in (Friedman 2007), which estimates a sparse inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$. Originally proposed by (Dempster 1972) under the name Covariance Selection, the framework has been expanded to include latent variables in (Chandrasekaran 2012) and more recently to jointly estimate multiple inverse covariance matrices, as seen in (Danaher 2013; Tomasi 2018). The GGLasso package supports the solution of a general formulation, encompassing significant special cases, including the single Graphical Lasso with latent variables, the Group, and the Fused Graphical Lasso.

By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, the authors' previous work on sampling accuracy has been expanded upon, allowing for the identification of stepsize-dependent biases in configurational averaging. For harmonic oscillators, certain schemes yield exact configurational averaging results, potentially leading to improved performance in biomolecular modeling, where bond stretches play a significant role. In general systems, an optimal method can be identified that exhibits very low bias in comparison to other alternatives. The optimal scheme proves to be a superior algorithm for molecular sampling, offering efficiency improvements of 25% or more in practical timestep sizes in vacuum and reductions in configurational average errors by a factor of ten or more in solvated simulations at large timesteps.

Therefore, a significant task involves identifying the appropriate configuration for the binary system and its environment at this point in the process. In our research, we've been investigating the behavior of dark matter in the vicinity of black hole binaries of equal mass, discovering a consistent, long-lasting profile that emerges over several orbits. Conversely, systems with greater dark matter mass see overdensities scattered due to the binary's motion. Furthermore, regardless of initial configurations, systems typically converge to the established profile after a certain number of orbits; this convergence often results in the emergence of undesirable, short-lived oscillations. It's also been found that if matter is directly overlaid onto a binary system, without properly considering the potential for matter to influence the binary's motion, this leads to inaccurately calculated orbital paths due to artificial factors, rather than a signature of dark matter in that realm, as previously reported; in fact, in such cases, the process of matter evaporating from the binary system is typically overly rapid. Lastly, further work is suggested to explore the establishment of the profile in greater detail, particularly in binary systems comprising three or more objects, as well as those that involve black holes of unequal mass.

In our approach, a network with multiple weighted and potentially directed graphs is analyzed, with each graph representing a separate network layer and no connections between them. The importance of each node in a given layer is determined by the weighted sum of the importance of adjacent nodes within that same layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality. However, our approach differs from the standard method in that the adjacency relationships and node importance can be derived from distinct layers. Unlike existing frameworks for multilayer eigenvector centrality that rely on connections between different layers, our model only partially incorporates inter-layer dependencies. The constrained, layer-specific eigenvector centrality values in our model are defined by a system of independent and dependent eigenvalue problems, which can be efficiently solved using a hybrid power iteration algorithm.

This surface seal is characterized by a distinct pattern of splash and cavity formation, and it can be divided into low-speed, high-speed, and intermediate regimes based on the sphere's velocity. Empirical laws governing the time it takes for the splash to collapse have been established for both low and high speeds, but there is a need for refinement in the transition between these regimes. Through the examination of extensive categories of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify the potential generalized global symmetries present and investigate the mechanisms by which they are circumvented. Key components of such effective field theories include generalized $\theta$-terms, which introduce non-linear interactions between axion fields and topological terms that are quadratic in gauge field strengths and which break a substantial portion of the global symmetries. Moreover, assuming the presence of charged states can lead to the breakdown of the remnant global symmetries. Nonetheless, we demonstrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms results in a generalized Witten effect, implying that the spectrum of charged states is composed of an infinitely populated grid. Furthermore, we show that this grid is generated by the action of the monodromy transformation that characterizes the boundary of the moduli space near which the effective theory is defined.

  Our objective is to minimize the number and intricacy of hardware and software components that a mobile user must trust to withstand malicious inputs. We propose a multi-domain hardware design consisting of isolated, statically-partitioned trust domains. To enable a program to temporarily access both processing and input/output functions simultaneously, we introduce a straightforward, statically-enforced policy. This policy allows programs to briefly combine trusted computation and untrusted user code.
  A key feature of this system is that external components can be automatically classified as either completely trusted or completely untrusted. For instance, a camera module might be an untrusted external component, whereas internal memory accessible to the operating system is a trusted domain.
  We have implemented a prototype of this system, called Tegl, on a single-core CPU SoC, and observed that it incurs a minimal hardware cost compared to contemporary CPUs. Our evaluation of the performance impact revealed that most performance-critical applications can run unaffected and that this system provides a reliable security against malicious programs despite a few notable limitations.

Our adversary model assumes a sophisticated opponent who can manipulate the reward and transition at any step within an episode, but only up to a certain percentage of episodes. Our model is more aggressive than previous approaches. We initially found that no algorithm can achieve a policy better than O(1/ε) competitive to the optimal policy, even when the reward corruption is as low as ε=10^-6. multi-phonon physics, is being explored for its potential applications in metrology and on-chip communication, among other areas. Quantum acoustic resonators, or cavities, are being utilized to investigate multi-phonon phenomena both theoretically and experimentally. We investigate a system consisting of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity. This system has exhibited intriguing multi-phonon effects, but previous descriptions have been limited to a two-level quantum dot model. This limitation restricts the complexity of a true semiconductor quantum dot. In this study, we propose a model that accounts for both bright and dark excitons in the quantum dot, with dark excitons being particularly useful due to their low decoherence rates. By fine-tuning the laser frequency, we demonstrate the ability to achieve giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles. Notably, in the absence of an external drive, we can spontaneously produce N-phonon bundles in the system from a dark exciton state alone, an achievement that has not been previously documented. This research opens up the possibility of observing phonon bundle emissions from a quantum dot driven by a laser.

lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, specifically the herringbone lattice with two orthogonal glide symmetries. We model this system using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model and find two distinct Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. Upon closer inspection, we reveal that various lattice distortions can modify the Dirac cones in Dirac-Weyl materials, with some motions destroying the Dirac cone structure. Next, we analyze the flow of electrons around the Dirac cones by calculating wave function amplitudes. We then explore the Dirac cone structure near the Dirac cones at the edge of the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path, revealing a transition from a plateaus-like to herringbone-like feature around the Dirac cones. Furthermore, we identify two distinct types of quasi-localized states: a herringbone-like state and a plateaus-like state, which depend on the distance from the Dirac cone. Additionally, we observe that the herringbone-like state has zero quasi-unitary folding transitions, in contrast to the plateaus-like state which has quasi-unitary folding transitions along high-symmetry paths.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis. This process utilizes a beam splitter (BS) or parametric amplifier (PA) to produce these states. SPCCSs are produced when a coherent state and a single-photon Fock state are input into a BS or PA, and a single photon is detected in one of the output channels. The probabilities of successful detection differ depending on whether BS or PA catalysis is used. It has been proven that SPCCSs generated by BS and PA devices are identical, as evidenced by their photon number distributions. Further analysis has revealed the non-Gaussian nature of SPCCSs, which exhibit sub-Poissionian distribution, anti-bunching, quadrature squeezing, and a negative Wigner function. These findings demonstrate the nonclassical properties of SPCCSs, which can be leveraged for various quantum technological applications.

We introduce a novel representation of polymers as combinations of monomers and develop new descriptors that capture their structural characteristics. Linear regression is used as a fundamental component in constructing predictive functions within the framework. Computational experiments demonstrate that the proposed approach effectively predicts certain chemical properties of polymers, particularly when the monomers contain up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms.

Due to the absence of a general analytical solution, numerical methods are employed to find approximate solutions. By adopting a standard notation, the paper discusses specific techniques used in the transcription process of simultaneous direct methods for solving dynamic optimization problems, specifically focusing on collocation, integrated residual, and Runge-Kutta schemes. These methods are then applied to a case study, which aimed to address a critical question that arose during the COVID-19 pandemic: whether it's feasible to ventilate patients using a single ventilator with specific characteristics, or if this would compromise the treatment's effectiveness. The resulting computations provided a crucial insight, revealing that it's theoretically possible to accomplish this task without compromising the treatment's efficacy, but further research is needed to confirm this outcome experimentally.

CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To overcome this, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. This study investigates whether it's possible to automate the process of segmenting esophageal tumors from CT scans alone. To achieve this, we developed a fully automatic method based on convolutional neural networks, called Dilated Dense Attention Unet (DDAUnet). This network utilizes spatial and channel attention gates to focus on the most relevant features and regions, and dilated convolutional layers to manage memory and increase the network's receptive field. We tested our method on a large dataset of 792 scans from 288 patients with varying anatomies and conditions, and the results showed a high degree of accuracy with a minimal number of parameters. Our code has been made publicly available for further research and development.

This process, known as geosteering, is typically supported by up-to-date formation evaluations obtained through well-log interpretation while drilling. For this application, a reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to analyze well logs and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary. An integrated iterative ensemble-based method, specifically the approximate Levenberg Marquardt form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML), is employed in our formation evaluation workflow. This method estimates model parameters, including resistivity, density, and boundary locations, along with their uncertainties, by minimizing the statistical discrepancy between the measurements from well logging tools and theoretical measurements from forward tool simulators. The accuracy and computational efficiency of the proposed method are demonstrated through the analysis of a synthetic case, showcasing its ability to handle petrophysical property variations. Additionally, the method's performance is evaluated under uncertain drilling conditions.

task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which do not adequately capture the hierarchical nature of nested entities. This work overcomes this limitation by modeling nested entities as an integrated whole and proposing a new parsing algorithm to accurately identify all entities at once. Microwave Background (CMB) could serve as evidence for the Conformal Cyclic Cosmology (CCC) model, which proposes the universe undergoes cycles of expansion and contraction. These patterns include low-variance circles resulting from black hole mergers and Hawking points resulting from black hole evaporation. A recent study used machine learning software called HawkingNet to search for Hawking points in the CMB, but found no statistically significant evidence. Similarly, a high-resolution search for low-variance circles in the Planck CMB map revealed no significant results after removing anomalies. However, the absence of distinct features in the CMB does not necessarily disprove CCC, as a large density of such patterns would produce a non-Gaussian fluctuation in the CMB. Interestingly, the real CMB sky exhibits a pronounced Gaussian offset compared to simulated Gaussian fluctuations. If the patterns predicted by CCC are densely populated, they should be evenly distributed and could potentially explain the anomalous offset in the CMB's Gaussian component. To confirm this, it would be essential to remove the Gaussian component from the CMB map and search for patterns in the residual map.

To achieve a meaningful detection of exoplanets orbiting low-mass stars, it is essential to analyze the activity noise in the radial velocity data sets. We conducted an analysis on how to optimize the selection of observations to minimize the standard deviation of the data sets, thereby enhancing the sensitivity of the method to detect subtle planetary signals. We tested different methods for selecting observations, including automated approaches and non-parametric models, and evaluated their effectiveness by applying them to real data from the M dwarfs survey. The analysis revealed that the automated selection of observations using the location adaptive median absolute deviation (LAMAD) algorithm yielded the lowest standard deviation of the data sets compared to other techniques. The LAMAD algorithm successfully minimized the activity noise, as confirmed by a residual activity test, and it is expected to improve the detection of planetary signals in future data sets from the M dwarfs survey. The optimal sampling strategy using the LAMAD algorithm achieved a sensitivity improvement of up to a factor of four compared to the original data sets, allowing for the detection of planets with masses 1.8 times that of the Earth orbiting closer to their host stars.

tool that significantly accelerates the creation of detailed cosmological simulations based on modified gravity theories. MG-GLAM is derived from the existing GLAM code and incorporates advanced algorithms to efficiently solve complex nonlinear equations characteristic of modified gravity models. This code is highly adaptable, allowing for simulations of various modified gravity theories, including f(R) gravity, symmetron, and coupled quintessence models. Its versatility and optimization have led to a substantial speed increase, making it capable of producing large-scale simulations that accurately predict the matter power spectrum and dark matter halo abundance. The simulations generated by MG-GLAM are invaluable for creating mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys.

extension that transforms a wiki into a collaborative workspace, ideal for crafting high-quality manuscripts and software projects. turbulent methane-air jet flame with the goal of predicting its response to upstream acoustic actuation, accounting for heat release fluctuations that are crucial for understanding thermoacoustic instabilities and flame noise in a linearized framework. An innovative approach in this study involves an active flame model that considers heat release oscillations caused by acoustic fluctuations. To implement this active flame approach in a linear framework, a combustion model needs to be linearized, which is achieved by developing and applying linearized Large Eddy Simulation and Direct Numerical Simulation combustion models. However, it is shown that these approaches lead to closure problems, making their application challenging. In contrast, Reynolds-averaged Navier Stokes combustion models prove to be linearizable and are used for the active flame approach. The linearized combustion models are applied to a realistic methane-air jet flame, which shows that the active flame approach can accurately replicate the flame structure and its oscillation dynamics when an acoustic perturbation is applied. Furthermore, an eigenvalue problem is solved to determine the flame's response to upstream acoustic actuation, which reveals that the active flame approach is capable of capturing both upstream and downstream flame propagation modes. The linearized model is used to investigate the impact of molecular diffusion on heat release oscillations, which shows that it has a significant impact on downstream propagation and the flame's response to acoustic actuation.

These clusters exhibit distinct and complex dynamics when compared to on-site clusters, which behave according to a different dynamics. Sites that belong to the same dynamic cluster can display anti-aliasing behavior, characterized by a unique symmetry in the site-bonding scheme. The dynamic cluster's effective repulsion and the resulting pair correlations can be interpreted within a simplified effective model, which reveals a broader cluster distribution with increasing temperature and spin imbalance, leading to a suppression of the symmetrized state at finite temperatures.

This interaction can be modeled as a classical field, resulting in a periodic modulation pattern of decay events. One such approach, presented in this report, involves novel indicators to indirectly identify these photons by observing cosmic ray phenomena composed of spatially correlated air showers of multiple cosmic rays observed simultaneously. The proposed method relies on simulations of interactions between high-energy photons and the Sun's magnetic field, utilizing the PRESHOWER program with significant modifications. The expected outcome of these interactions includes the creation of cosmic ray ensembles consisting of extremely narrow and elongated cascades of secondary photons spanning the full cosmic ray energy spectrum. When entering the Earth's atmosphere, these cascades or their components might generate distinct walls of spatially correlated air showers, which could also occur even if the primary photons are not directed towards Earth. Furthermore, it is anticipated that particle distributions within these multi-photon footprints will possess thicknesses of approximately meters and extensions of up to hundreds of millions of kilometers, rendering them potentially observable with a collaborative global approach, incorporating re-evaluation of historical data and exceeding the capacity of even the largest cosmic ray observatories. The quantities in question involve new dimensions of observability that go beyond the capabilities of simulations like PRESHOWER, which only model particle densities in depth, assuming instantaneous exposures and lacking the rigor to tackle footprints of universal cosmic ray ensembles properly.

The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties. A simplified approach yields a theory identical to the nonlocal gravity theory proposed earlier by M. Blagojevic and F. Rudijck, albeit without resorting to an ad-hoc assumption. Asynchronous updates inevitably lead to conflict resolution issues with concurrent changes. A specific technique addressing this challenge is the Conflict-free Replicated Data Type (CRDT). Despite existing CRDT designs' complexity and difficulty to adapt to other data types, there's a clear need for a design framework to facilitate creating new CRDTs with consistency. -wide association studies (GWAS) can be facilitated by identifying relevant annotations. We've developed a statistical model that leverages genome-wide association data to pinpoint genomic elements that significantly influence traits, incorporating diverse types of annotations. This model was applied to 18 human traits, examining 450 different annotations, such as genes, enhancers, and chromatin sites in various tissues and cell lines. the Galactic Centre region, which have shown no signs of outbursts over a decade of monitoring, have led researchers to suggest the presence of a significant population of stellar mass black holes in this area. A key component of the argument that these objects are actively accreting black holes is the claim that neutron stars in low-mass X-ray binaries typically do not experience prolonged intervals between outbursts. This paper challenges this assertion by showing that nearly half of the known transient LMXBs with confirmed neutron star primaries exhibit recurrence times exceeding a decade for outbursts detectable by MAXI. Furthermore, to reconcile the total number of neutron star LMXBs with observed and predicted outburst rates, it is necessary to assume that the majority of these systems have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts observable by MAXI, and that only a small fraction of these systems have been discovered thus far.

To assess the feasibility of this test, I employed a specific method that involves analyzing only the velocity components within a specific plane in the sky. This analysis was applied to a dataset of binary star systems from a study by Hernandez et. al. (2019), taking into account potential distortions caused by large angles. According to simulations, the uncertainty in measuring velocity dispersion using projected velocities is approximately 100 meters per second, but this decreases to around 30 meters per second when using line velocities, which are less affected by distance uncertainties. However, my analysis of the data revealed that the applicability of the velocity dispersion test is limited to a specific range of binary star systems with particular properties. Furthermore, a comparison of the test results with predictions based on the law of gravity revealed that it fails to explain the data with a high degree of confidence, but this failure may be attributed to uncertainties in the measurements. To achieve a decisive outcome, it is necessary to increase the size of the dataset by a factor of ten.

Understanding the polarization properties of these sources in relation to their characteristics is essential for various applications. This study examines the median fractional polarization of radio sources with 1.4 GHz flux density between 6.6 and 70 mJy by analyzing the polarized intensity from the FIRST survey. The results reveal that the median fractional polarization is strongly related to the angular size of sources smaller than 5" and weakly related to larger sources. Additionally, the curvature of the low-frequency radio spectrum is inversely correlated with the median fractional polarization, indicating a connection between depolarization and the source itself.

By applying approximate adiabatic invariants, we expand the classical equal-area method in both integral and differential forms. We predict shock behavior for finite wave trains with a sinusoidal shape, providing distinct solutions for internal shocks, head shocks, and tail shocks, and confirming these predictions with numerical simulations. Our internal shock solution leads to revised expressions for shock heating rates, while our head and tail shock solution reveals their capacity to preserve the energy released by the shock at larger radii. -mass stellar objects may be impacted by rotation due to the influence of centrifugal force on their equilibrium and the possibility of mass loss through rotational break-up. We have created numerical models of rotating low-mass stars to examine their ability to sustain nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates that result in significant deformation. Critical boundaries defining the conditions for sustainable hydrogen burning have been identified in terms of mass and central degeneracy for various levels of angular momentum. Our findings indicate that when the angular momentum surpasses a certain threshold, the critical boundary splits into two distinct regions with lower and higher degeneracy due to mass loss. Based on these results, we have modeled the thermal and mechanical evolution of substellar objects, taking into account cooling, mass loss, and angular momentum reduction. Two scenarios have been explored: one involving external braking mechanisms, such as magnetized winds, which dictate the spin-down timescale, and the other where mass loss occurs through gravitational contraction, often accompanied by the formation of a ring or disc, as seen in the SZ Psc system.

groups of objects have numerous practical applications, and their visualization often takes the form of a 2-tier layout where corresponding entities are aligned horizontally across two parallel lines, connected by lines representing relationships between them. research introduces a new technique called HyperDegrade, which combines existing methods with the use of multi-threading architectures. Alongside the new technique, the study identifies the underlying causes of performance degradation through cache eviction and uncovers a previously unknown source of slowdown. The resulting slowdown is significantly higher than previous methods, leading to a finer time granularity for Flush+Reload attacks. The effectiveness of HyperDegrade is demonstrated on various Intel microarchitectures, yielding substantial slowdowns that achieve significant improvements over current state-of-the-art methods. To evaluate the performance degradation's impact on side-channel amplification, the study proposes and assesses leakage assessment metrics, which show that HyperDegrade increases time granularity without compromising trace quality. Furthermore, the research compares three performance degradation strategies in conjunction with Flush+Reload attacks from an attacker's perspective and showcases HyperDegrade's efficacy in predicting Rounding Cup Size on actual microarchitectures. To mitigate HyperDegrade-like performance degradations, the study provides strategies for countermeasures.

explain the muon's anomalous magnetic moment, we employed an Effective Field Theory (EFT) approach. Although the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment is minimal, a bottom-up EFT analysis reveals that the Higgs could still resolve the anomaly if its interactions with other SM particles deviate from their predicted values. Applying unitarity principles, we found that such a solution would imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of around 10-18 TeV, which could be lowered to 5 TeV if the Higgs interactions with the W and Z bosons conform to SM expectations. This scenario could lead to a notable increase in di-Higgs production in muon colliders, making it a compelling reason to investigate further. Ultimately, this study underscores the importance of measuring the Higgs coupling to the muon and Higgs in future experiments.

as an unknotting operation. Any given knot diagram can be transformed into an unknot diagram by applying a series of unknotting operations in conjunction with some Reidemeister moves. Moreover, they also have substantial applications in biology, chemistry, and physics for studying intricate string entanglements, organic compound structures, and DNA configurations. In this research, we introduced a novel unknotting operation, the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. Additionally, we defined a distance metric based on the diagonal move and investigated its characteristics.

problem design holds significant importance. Various disciplines like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning extensively employ matrix operations to resolve complex issues. To mitigate this, the integration of parallel computing techniques, such as CUDA and openMP, has become essential. This study compares sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication, with findings indicating that parallel processing has a profound impact on computational efficiency, particularly with larger matrices.

We investigate how a group of rational agents decide which of several tasks to undertake when the tasks' difficulty levels are uncertain and only partially known. We demonstrate the existence of a Nash equilibrium with a straightforward, linear pattern under certain conditions. Furthermore, under the requirement that agents act in accordance with the minimax rule, we show that the optimal action for each agent is the solution to a linear programming problem. Last, in scenarios where all possible task difficulties can be fully assessed, we establish the criteria for a set of linear inequalities that define the Coarse Corpuscular Multi-Armed Bandit problem as a problem that can be efficiently resolved via standard computational methods.

study, we concentrate on vertical federated learning (VFL), which allows multiple entities to jointly train a robust machine learning model using shared features, without exchanging sensitive information. Based on collaboration patterns, VFL can be distinguished from horizontal federated learning. Our focus is on identifying potential privacy breaches in real-world VFL systems. To achieve this, we have developed and implemented two real-world privacy attacks: a reverse multiplication attack targeting the logistic regression VFL protocol, and a reverse sum attack targeting the XGBoost VFL protocol. Our empirical results demonstrate that the attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and diverse, and can successfully compromise the privacy of real-world VFL systems. The findings indicate that private VFL protocols are vulnerable to privacy breaches, and our techniques can be applied to assess the privacy of VFL protocols. Consequently, we emphasize the importance of formulating robust privacy-preserving VFL protocols.

To address this limitation, Random Fourier Features (RFF) was introduced as a method to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on large datasets. However, despite its popularity, RFF has certain drawbacks, including the need for a large number of feature expansions that is directly proportional to the dataset size. This necessitates a reduction in feature dimensions to achieve effective scalability. In response, this paper presents a novel kernel approximation method called Pseudo Random Fourier Features (PRFF), which adapts to the specific characteristics of the training data and aims to improve prediction performance by decreasing the number of feature dimensions. The proposed approach is evaluated and compared with other methods, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström approach, on classification and regression tasks.

We first categorize and explicitly describe conformally flat hypersurfaces of dimension $n$ or higher with constant M\"obius curvature under the M\"obius transformation group of the sphere. Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily relies on ventricular volume and function according to current clinical guidelines. These biomarkers can be accurately assessed through 3D cardiac magnetic resonance image segmentation. Recent studies have shown that U-Net architectures have achieved impressive results on various datasets. However, in real-world clinical settings, data sets are more diverse and influenced by individual pathologies, scanner properties, and limited training data for rare conditions like Tetralogy of Fallot. This work investigates two aspects: the accuracy gap when training models on one dataset (ACDC) and applying them to another (TOF), and whether similar results can be achieved when applying models to a more heterogeneous dataset. Multiple deep learning models were trained and evaluated using four-fold cross-validation, demonstrating that models can achieve excellent results within a single dataset but struggle with overfitting when applied to other pathologies, resulting in significantly reduced dice scores for both left and right ventricles.

The system is designed to collect energy from an access point without the need for a splitter, utilizing a unique architecture that separates the spectrum for information and energy harvesting in an OFDMA network. To evaluate the benefits, an optimization problem is formulated to maximize energy harvesting in a multi-user OFDMA network while ensuring minimum data rates for all users. Pyramid Networks (FPNs), have been facing a long-standing challenge. Researchers have observed that the performance of FPN-based detectors tends to decline for large-scale objects. This paper re-examines FPN's role in the detection framework, attributing its success to optimization perspectives. It also identifies the root cause of the decreased performance as the emergence of improper back-propagation paths after integrating FPN, which restricts each backbone level to focus on specific scale ranges. To address this issue, two strategies are proposed to enable each backbone level to consider all objects within the FPN-based frameworks. Firstly, auxiliary objective functions are introduced to facilitate direct back-propagation signals for various-scale objects during training. Secondly, a more rational feature pyramid construction method is proposed to eliminate irrational back-propagation paths. Experimental results on the COCO benchmark validate the analysis and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed methods, yielding significant improvements (over 2%) in various detection frameworks, including one-stage, two-stage, anchor-based, anchor-free, and transformer-based detectors.

Given an irreducible simple algebraic group G and a Borel subgroup B, consider an irreducible subgroup P containing B, and let P' be its derived group. A theorem by Richardson states that the algebra of P semi-invariants is multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety e+V that induces an isomorphism between the algebra of P semi-invariants and the algebra of e+V is called a Weierstrass section. In this work, a Weierstrass section is constructed in type A, with a focus on its application rather than its construction. The nilfibre relative to the action of P is denoted by N, and it is shown that a point e in N can be used to describe the structure of a unique irreducible component C of N. The description of e+V provides an explicit characterization of C as a B saturation set, which is a subalgebra of the Lie algebra of the nilradical of B. However, this subalgebra may not be complemented, and therefore, C may not be an orbital variety closure. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that C can be empty, and this is shown to occur in a specific example in A10.

This work introduces a novel stochastic hydrodynamic method, based on the positive-P phase-space formalism, to model interacting Bose gases. This method surpasses existing approaches in its ability to simulate the full quantum behavior of these systems, including non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. A linearized version of the method is derived, allowing for longer simulations of non-equilibrium situations while approximating quantum fluctuations. The current approaches, which rely on matching boundaries, generate numerous proposals but fail to capture the broader context surrounding the action. Moreover, densely generated matchings lack the semantic richness required for accurate action detection. To address this issue, we introduce the Dual Context Aggregation Network (DCAN), an end-to-end proposal generation method that aggregates context on two levels: boundary and proposal. The context is extracted from the surrounding frames and proposals, then incorporated into boundary-specific matchings, which are subsequently used to generate action proposals with start and end times. By incorporating a context aggregation module with two distinct aggregations and a matching boundary module, DCAN leverages both frame and proposal context for improved action detection. The ablated experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of enhancing context aggregations and the superiority of our approach over the baseline methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance on ActivityNet v1.3, with an average mAP of 35.39%. The code for DCAN is publicly available at https://github.com/cg1177/DCAN.

Research typically attributes the PTM's origin to magnetic field ergodisation and the emergence of a seed island. However, this study proposes an alternative explanation based on edge plasma turbulence principles. Observations of plasma turbulence reveal the existence of coherent structures called blobs and holes in the scrape-off-layer. These structures exhibit higher or lower plasma densities and carry parallel currents. By interpreting ELM filaments as massive blobs and the interspace as holes, the study demonstrates that a closed current filament can produce similar magnetic fluctuations as measured by the JET in-vessel coils. This suggests that capturing a hole on a q=3 surface after an ELM crash can generate a PTM equivalent signature, while capturing the ELM filament itself on a q=4 surface produces an outer mode signature.

This method fosters a cooperative behavior among robots, ensuring they avoid each other reciprocally. The repulsive field of a robot is activated when it detects the vorticity field created by other robots. The absence of local minima is guaranteed through the design of the repulsive field's potential energy function. The annealed large deviation principle for the empirical process of words involves a rate function that is the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words relative to the reference distribution of words. In a previous study, the quenched large deviation principle was derived for renewal times with an algebraic tail, resulting in a rate function consisting of two terms: the annealed rate function and a term proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by concatenating words and randomizing the origin. This study aims to extend both large deviation principles to non-i.i.d. letter sequences by demonstrating that they remain valid under a condition known as summable variation. The resulting rate functions are specific relative entropies with respect to the reference distributions of words and letters, which are not necessarily i.i.d. This requires several approximation arguments to achieve the extension.

growing interest in the intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) technology. This technology utilizes passive reflective elements capable of adjusting the phase, amplitude, frequency, and polarization of incoming waveforms. Given its desirable properties, the characteristics of wireless channels can be manipulated to meet specific signal requirements, holding great promise for radar applications. This paper lays the theoretical groundwork for integrating IRS into radar systems and explores its potential to improve target parameter estimation. Specifically, we examine the deployment of IRS in scenarios where the line-of-sight (LOS) link is weak or obstructed by an obstacle. We demonstrate that IRS can establish a virtual, non-line-of-sight (NLOS) link between the radar and target, leading to enhanced radar performance. Numerical simulations reveal that the effectiveness of this virtual link in estimating target parameters is improved when the LOS link is significantly weaker than the NLOS link, with a relative strength ratio of approximately $10^{-1}$.

In software testing, mutation analysis is the benchmark for evaluating test quality by assessing the ability of a test to detect artificial bugs; if a set of tests fails to detect such mutations, it will also fail to detect actual bugs. This method encompasses various coverage measures and provides a diverse set of faults that can be difficult to fail, making it a comprehensive and challenging test set. However, the traditional mutation analysis approach is impractical for fuzzing due to the high cost of independent evaluation. In software testing, multiple independent evaluations are combined to evaluate a testing technique, but for fuzzing, a single, extensive input is typically sufficient to determine program crashes. This paper proposes an innovative mutation analysis approach for fuzzing, which leverages multiple independent mutations to evaluate a fuzzer. We demonstrate how this approach can be applied to cover mutations in various data types and how it can be used to evaluate and compare fuzzers using actual mutations.

Some of these approaches build upon the pre-trained representations by introducing minimal or no updates to the backbone models during the training process. This paper challenges the necessity of complex models in achieving high performance by comparing them to a simple baseline. We propose that a pre-trained feature extractor can be a robust tool for achieving competitive or superior continual learning results on the Split-CIFAR100 and CoRe 50 benchmarks. To validate this, we introduce a straightforward baseline that 1) employs a frozen pre-trained model to extract image features for each class encountered during the continual learning stage and computes the mean features from the training data, and 2) predicts the class of the input based on the nearest neighbor distance between test samples and the mean features of the classes; namely, the Nearest Mean Classifier (NMC). This baseline is single-headed, exemplar-free, and can be task-free, with the means being updated continually. The baseline achieved 88.53% on the 10-Split-CIFAR-100, outperforming most state-of-the-art continual learning methods that are all initialized using the same pre-trained transformer model. We hope our baseline will encourage future advancements in designing learning systems that can continually enhance learning representations even when starting from pre-trained weights.

They demonstrated that these games allow for the existence of $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibria under specific conditions for $\epsilon$ and $\lambda$. However, they also posed an question regarding the speed at which one can find such an equilibrium, which, in conjunction with a related problem of value approximation, was answered in the context of subgame perfect equilibria for the case of binary actions. This paper addresses the same questions for broader classes of games with arbitrary action spaces, particularly focusing on finding an equilibrium or an equilibrium's value, in the context of multi-player games. The obtained results depend on the dimension of the action space's convex domain and $\lambda$-Lipschitz property, providing a solution to a problem left open by the problem's original formulation. Furthermore, the paper presents a reduction from finding an equilibrium to value approximation, and presents an algorithm that combines a sequence of two existing algorithms to find an $\epsilon$-approximate pure Nash equilibrium in polynomial time. An additional contribution of the paper is the identification of a new class of games with the property that they have an $\epsilon$-approximate correlated equilibrium that can be found in polynomial time. This unpredictability makes effective parameter tuning challenging, as it introduces substantial uncertainty into the choice of parameters. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. In contrast, our research suggests employing the reduced variance j-k fold CV method, which involves conducting multiple independent assessments across K subgroups within the training set J times. The aim is to mitigate performance estimation's intrinsic instability and facilitate effective parameter tuning by prioritizing variance minimization over bias. In line with this principle, our study advocates for a smaller K than typically adopted and instead invests computational resources in increasing the value of J, as this yields more dependable optimal parameter configurations than increased training data alone.

This approach has been successfully applied to various knowledge learning objectives such as knowledge distillation, expansion, adaptation, and multi-task learning. Current research utilizes Teacher-Student architectures to achieve multiple knowledge-learning objectives through lightweight and effective student networks. This paper provides a detailed discussion on Teacher-Student architectures with multiple knowledge learning objectives and systematically explains the knowledge construction and optimization process during knowledge learning. ices exhibits a peculiar response to a temperature gradient applied along its length, resulting in the generation of an electric field perpendicular to the gradient. This phenomenon reaches its maximum intensity at a specific temperature and magnetic field strength, which likely corresponds to the point where the entropy difference between the central region of the vortex and its surroundings is most pronounced. Notably, the magnitude of this peak is strikingly consistent across a wide range of superconducting materials, suggesting a common underlying mechanism. This peak can be interpreted as the point at which the ratio of viscosity to entropy density within the vortex liquid is minimized. When expressed in terms of the fundamental constants $\hbar$ and $k_B$, this minimum is found to be significantly larger than what is observed in ordinary liquids. Furthermore, the entropy stored within the central region of the vortex is distinct from that associated with a moving magnetic field line, due to the exchange of normal particles that can occur between the vortex and its surroundings. As a result, a slowly moving vortex will tend to lose its associated entropy over a distance comparable to the coherence length of the superconducting material, provided that the ratio of the energy gap to the Fermi energy is sufficiently large.

Current methods of assessing this flexibility are often based on slow-moving estimations, with less attention paid to real-time coordination between aggregators and the grid operator. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem in a closed-loop system, where the grid operator can interact with aggregators in real-time to ensure the feasibility of the controllable loads they manage. We also introduce a real-time communication protocol that enables the grid operator to query the flexibility of individual aggregators, with the aggregators responding based on their current knowledge of the system state. To facilitate this process, we discuss possible methods for aggregators to estimate the temporal variation in the flexibility of the loads they manage. The key contribution of this paper is the introduction of an efficient algorithm for a scenario with no prior knowledge, where the communication with the grid operator is binary, with the potential for the aggregators to perform more complex queries under higher communication limits. The benefits of this approach are illustrated through simulations on a test network.

ysics is the common envelope phase of binary star evolution, where two stars are enveloped by the outer layer of one of them. As the stars interact with the envelope, the orbit shrinks due to the intense interactions. This phase can ultimately lead to the merging of the stars or a subsequent series of interactions. Mergers involving compact objects, such as white dwarfs, neutron stars, or black holes, can produce a range of spectacular astrophysical events, including supernovae, gamma-ray bursts, and gravitational waves. Due to the diversity of initial conditions and the complexity of the processes involved, predicting the final state of common envelope phases is challenging. In large-scale calculations, such as population synthesis models, conservation laws are often employed. This study develops a novel approach to utilizing angular momentum to derive a simplified formula for the final orbital separation in common envelope phases, offering advantages in the study of binary and multiple star systems, particularly in the context of potential mergers. This work primarily focuses on common envelope phases in binary star systems, while a companion paper extends the methodology to more complex multiple star systems.

the calculation of localized shock collisions in a five-dimensional space that is asymptotically Anti-de Sitter. By expanding the Einstein equations in terms of transverse gradients, it's found that numerical results match exact solutions at the first order of expansion. The Einstein equations at this order can be broken down into two sets of differential equations, where one set's bulk fields contribute negligibly to boundary observables. This simplifies computations to solving planar shockwave equations and a few additional differential equations for each 'pixel' in a transverse plane. The framework achieves a significant speedup of roughly one order of magnitude, with errors of less than 10% at the hydrodynamization time and for low to mid rapidities.

we've analyzed the large-scale structure of ionized and molecular gas in the starbursting galaxy IRAS08339+6517, located 500 parsecs in size. Our study has uncovered a direct relationship between the mass flux of star formation-driven gas outflows and the galaxy's star formation rate. The data suggest that outflows are closely linked to the galaxy's ability to recycle gas, with areas of high star formation rates expelling more gas than they consume through star formation. These findings support the idea that outflows play a crucial role in regulating the galaxy's ability to sustain short gas depletion times. Our results highlight the importance of further studies on gas outflows in galaxies to better understand their role in galaxy evolution.

Recently, Structured Bayesian Optimization (SBO) has successfully addressed these difficulties by utilizing probabilistic models. SBO achieves fast convergence by breaking down the parameter space using contextual information from system experts. However, the complexity of building probabilistic models has limited its widespread adoption. To address this issue, we introduce BoAnon, a SBO framework that learns the system's structure from its logs. Compared to existing methods, BoAnon achieves significant improvements in solution quality, with optimization times that are several orders of magnitude lower.

time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) lies in maintaining the integrity of specific properties inherent to the continuous solution, such as underlying conservation laws or geometric structures. Researchers have been studying structure-preserving discretisation schemes for a considerable amount of time, including verifying that conventional methods retain these properties and proposing innovative schemes that achieve both high accuracy and exact preservation of certain properties of the underlying differential equation. However, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, these schemes have a significant drawback: their ability to preserve structure relies on the exact solution of the systems of equations defining each time-step in the discrete scheme. Although this is feasible for small systems, it becomes impractical for large linear systems resulting from typical discretisation of space-time PDEs. This paper proposes an adjustment to the flexible generalised minimum residual (FGMRES) iteration that enforces selected constraints on approximate numerical solutions, and demonstrates its application to both conservation laws and dissipative systems.

Our simulations reveal that in the absence of external pressure, superbubbles

However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining far-field 3D annotations, particularly from lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Current 3D detection metrics employ a one-size-fits-all approach, which is inconsistent with the principle of relative scaling in computer vision. As a result, the Far3Det task is not thoroughly analyzed. For instance, the conventional wisdom that high-resolution sensors are crucial for detecting far-away objects is contradicted by the current benchmark leaderboards, suggesting that depth sensors with higher resolution do not necessarily perform better in the far-field. To address this question, a new evaluation protocol is proposed for the Far3D detection task, which includes a revised metric and a more robust evaluation strategy. A comprehensive study is conducted on the nuScenes dataset, demonstrating that high-resolution depth sensors do enhance Far3D detection, even accounting for the cost of point processing. The best far-field detection metric is also introduced, which activates the detector at various distances, eliminating the risk of over-optimization. A state-of-the-art detector, the anchor-free MS3D proposal generator, is designed to tackle the Far3D detection task

the potential energy surface (PES) of molecules, which represents their energy levels in relation to their nuclear positions. Nevertheless, calculating this data is complex due to the vast number of ground states and the high-dimensional nature of the PES, making it difficult to prepare the required quantum states. This research introduces a novel approach using a generative quantum machine learning model that enables the preparation of ground states for a broad range of molecular data without needing full-dimensional quantum calculations. This method utilizes a quantum neural network to analyze a two-dimensional slice of the PES and then applies a quantum conditional-sampling protocol to produce ground states across the entire potential energy space. By integrating a classical optimization algorithm, a pre-trained model can be optimized to replicate ground states at specific points on the PES. Our findings demonstrate that this approach can efficiently prepare ground states for hydrogen chains, including the difficult H4 case, and promises significant improvements in the quantum simulation of chemical reactions and other complex molecular transformations.

The framework generates 3D bounding boxes around moving objects and estimates their motion trajectories. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This has allowed us to develop a list of 11 non-bipartite cubic graphs, including papillon graphs, snakes, and wheelfaces, whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of their 3-edge-colouring. Furthermore, we introduce a new family of papillon graphs, referred to as double papillon graphs, and establish that these and certain other non-bipartite cubic graphs possess the Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property.

Two alternative techniques, wavefield reconstruction inversion (WRI) and extended source waveform inversion (ESI), have been developed to overcome this limitation. WRI and ESI are formulated within a unified mathematical framework, utilizing a Lagrangian-based adjoint-state method with a focus on time-domain formulations and extended sources. By selectively pumping a nonlinear resonator with a coherent field, we induce a chiral interaction between the resonators, allowing us to create an all-optical diode and a three-port circulator. This chiral coupling enables our device to work with both single-photon pulses and strong light, offering an isolation ratio of over 40 dB and fidelity of more than 98%. Firstly, we develop metrics to measure the Bperp bias, assessing its impact on both local and global components. To address this, we investigated the mechanisms behind rumor dissemination and developed a method to measure the impact of a rumor based on its propagation speed. The frequency of searches related to the rumor served as a key indicator. By analyzing the peak and attenuation rates, which follow an exponential distribution, we identified crucial features and applied them to a predictive model. Our results, obtained through a 5-fold cross-validation experiment, revealed that decision trees are effective for predicting peak rates, while linear regression models perform best for predicting attenuation rates. Our analysis also highlighted the significance of precursor features in determining the peak rate, whereas location and entity information are more relevant for predicting the attenuation rate. Notably, features that facilitate the initial spread of a rumor often hinder its continued dissemination. Additionally, anxiety was found to be a critical factor contributing to the spread of rumors. Finally, we discuss the potential of utilizing the BERT model to minimize forecast errors and improve the accuracy of rumor prediction.

The crystallization process significantly affects a polymer's mechanical and thermal properties, necessitating consideration in both manufacturing and application design. To comprehensively capture its effects, the proposed model employs a unique decomposition of the deformation gradient and integrates a thermodynamic framework for material modeling. This framework relies on the Coleman-Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle, which in turn requires specific assumptions about the Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential. The resulting model is capable of simulating crystalline region formation and degradation, as well as temperature changes during deformation. For instance, in robotics, guiding a robotic manipulator through kinesthetic demonstrations demands the teacher to simultaneously control multiple degrees of freedom, making it a difficult task. The necessity for optimal demonstrations severely restricts the scope of problems where a teacher can provide quality feedback. To overcome this limitation, an alternative approach is to have the teacher provide corrective feedback, such as preferences or rewards, rather than demonstrations. While prior work has developed algorithms that can learn from specific types of noisy feedback, there is a need for a more general framework that can accommodate a variety of feedback types from different teachers and tasks. To address this challenge, we propose a new approach that models a stream of feedback as a series of loss functions, allowing us to use online learning algorithms to minimize the sum of these losses. By doing so, we can learn from a diversity of weakly correlated feedback. Our proposed meta-algorithm unifies prior work and demonstrates that it can achieve the same regret bounds regardless of the type of feedback. We evaluate our approach by training a robotic racecar to navigate a household environment, and our results show that it can learn efficiently from a variety of noisy feedback.

This was achieved by analyzing the noise kernels associated with the stress-energy tensor of quantum fields. This paper posits that rain generation and removal are interconnected processes that should be treated as a single, cohesive unit. To achieve this, we propose a novel approach that involves jointly learning the procedures for generating and removing rain within a unified image translation framework. Our proposed model, a bidirectional disentangled translation network, consists of two unidirectional networks, each comprising two loops that handle both real and synthetic rain images. We employ a disentanglement strategy that decomposes rainy images into clean backgrounds and rain layers, enabling better preservation of background information through the use of cycle-consistency and adversarial losses. This approach simplifies the translation of rain layers between real and synthetic rain images. Conversely, a counterpart composition with an entanglement strategy is applied for rain generation. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through extensive experiments on both rain generation and removal tasks, outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods on the challenging task of removing real rain from images.

unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following advancements are presented:

  - Enhanced Security: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security, meeting minimal cryptographic requirements for both public-key and private-key settings.
  - Improved Lower Bound and Generalized Construction: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a success probability of $0.85^n$. A generalized construction based on a broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is proposed, along with cloning attacks achieving probabilities of $0.71^n$ and $0.75^n$ against specific schemes.
  - Implications for Copy-Protection: Unclonable encryption satisfying a stronger property, unclonable-indistinguishability, implies copy-protection for a specific class of unlearnable functions. Although current encryption schemes do not meet this criterion, this connection offers a new path to construct copy-protection mechanisms.

The analysis involves a model comprising an encoder, decoder, and adversary, with the latter having access to the message, a non-causal noisy transmission observation, and unlimited transmission capabilities. The presence of lattice relaxation in the sample causes the flat band to blend with remote valence bands, leading to significant differences in the contribution of interband transitions to the plasmon dispersion and energy. Under conditions where only intraband transitions within the doped flat band are considered, low-damped and quasi-flat plasmons arise. Conversely, a $\sqrt q$ plasmon dispersion is observed when interband transitions between the flat band and remote bands are also taken into account. The plasmon energies can be adjusted through twist angles and doping levels. However, in rigid samples without lattice relaxation, both conditions can coexist, allowing for quasi-flat plasmons and interband transitions at larger momenta. For highly doped rigid samples, enhanced interband transitions can suppress the quasi-flat plasmon. Our study highlights the importance of two key factors, a isolated flat band and a suitable hole-doping level, for observing quasi-flat plasmons in twisted bilayer transition metal dichalcogenides.

an expansive outflow of material, often funneled by magnetic fields into surrounding magnetospheres. The powerful winds of massive stars are generated by the scattering of radiative energy, whereas in smaller stars like the Sun, weaker mass loss occurs due to the thermal expansion of heated coronas. In exoplanets orbiting these low-mass stars, radiative heating and wind interaction can cause atmospheric expansion or erosion. Stellar magnetospheres form internally due to wind trapping, whereas planetary magnetospheres are shaped by external stellar wind impacts. However, in both cases, stress can trigger magnetic reconnection, producing observable phenomena like X-ray flares and radio bursts. This review aims to provide an overview of the underlying physics of these processes, highlighting their similarities and differences in stars and planets.

As the thickness of the Bismuth layer is reduced, the magnetic anisotropy of resistivity increases, reaching a maximum at a Bismuth thickness of 0.6 monolayers. This behavior may be attributed to the interplay between the Bismuth layers and the surrounding Cobalt layers. Our research highlights the complexity of the Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and motivates further research to understand and control Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity.

To this end, we calculate the precise corrections to a specific particle reaction at the LHC, achieving a high level of accuracy through advanced computational methods. A dedicated tool is developed to evaluate these corrections in real-time during event simulation. We analyze the effects of these corrections on particle behavior, known as neutrino properties, in two distinct scenarios. Our results are expressed in two ways: a new formula for the neutrino mass, and a modification of the standard model's predicted behavior. With the correct treatment of these corrections, we can accurately recreate observed particle reactions. A previous underestimate of these corrections led to an overprediction of certain neutrino properties. Our new results are robust and can be used to reanalyze existing experimental data. For certain particle configurations, the corrections are significant, meaning that existing experimental limitations need to be reassessed. Our new formula for the neutrino mass will be crucial for future analyses. With these corrections, the proposed LHC upgradings will be able to precisely measure this property. Our study highlights the importance of accurately modeling particle reactions, particularly when lepton-flavour non-universality is in play.

Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. This behavior is connected to the eigenvalue distribution of the associated universal algebra, and we demonstrate that the complexity of this subspace can be quantified by the entropy of its eigenvalues. Analyzing spectral energy distributions and radial velocity variations could aid in identifying possible artificial structures, such as Dyson Spheres.

A distributed, hierarchical approach to SLA monitoring has been previously proposed, utilizing an overlay network of nodes that each represent a subset of SLA objectives. In this article, a quorum-based distributed control system is designed, utilizing a hierarchical network of nodes that execute partial control logic. The quorum method ensures decisions are made when a super-majority of nodes agrees, achieving high reliability in the system. However, this approach leads to complex data exchanges between nodes, which can cause delays and difficulties in scaling. To address these limitations, a novel strategy is presented that utilizes asynchronous communications, combining the benefits of a quorum-based system with the flexibility of a hierarchical network. This new approach enables a more efficient and scalable implementation of the distributed control logic, eliminating the need for exchanging raw data among nodes. Instead, a node can initiate an update if it holds a quorum, achieving a synchronization event and updating the underlying database accordingly. This modification enhances the system's performance, efficiency, and scalability. To validate the benefits of this architecture, a prototype and simulation were developed using Python, a quorum-based distributed database, and the ONEMedia monitoring framework. The upcoming generation of long-baseline neutrino experiments features near detectors consisting of three-dimensional projection scintillator trackers, which boast superior timing resolution and fine granularity, enabling them to measure neutron kinetic energy in real-time for each interaction. In this study, we investigated how the presence of surface water impacts these particles. Typically, laboratory conditions involve multiple water layers on the grains, but in the low-pressure environment of protoplanetary discs and moderate temperatures, grains likely only have a single water layer. As dust moves inward, even this layer eventually evaporates in higher temperature zones. To account for this, we re-examined the tensile strength of the same chondritic material we previously studied under normal laboratory conditions, but this time using two new preparation methods: drying the dust in air (dry samples) and heating it in a vacuum (super-dry samples). For temperatures up to 1000 K, our data for dry samples showed that their sticking forces increased by approximately ten times compared to wet samples. Up to 900 K, super-dry samples behaved similarly to dry samples. However, their sticking forces then increased exponentially to another factor of approximately 100 at about 1200 K. The increase in sticking from wet to dry samples follows a trend observed in amorphous silicates and extends to multimineral mixtures. The findings for super-dry dust suggest that aggregate growth is enhanced in a small, high-temperature region around 1200 K, which could be a favorable environment for planetesimal formation.

ymmetric spin-orbit coupling and exposed to a Zeeman magnetic field may serve as a viable pathway to achieving superconducting states with non-Abelian topological order and thereby enabling robust and efficient quantum computation. Employing a quantum Monte Carlo dynamical cluster approximation, we investigated the superconducting properties of a two-dimensional attractive Hubbard model with Rashba spin-orbit coupling and a Zeeman magnetic field. Our findings indicate that Rashba spin-orbit coupling has a positive impact on s-wave superconductivity. When superconductivity is suppressed by the Zeeman field due to Pauli pair-breaking, the Rashba coupling counteracts the spin imbalance caused by the Zeeman field by mixing the spins, thus restoring superconductivity at finite temperatures. This favorable effect of the spin-orbit coupling arises from a spin-flip driven enhancement of the amplitude for the propagation of a pair of electrons in time-reversed states. Furthermore, we discovered that for sufficiently large Rashba coupling and Zeeman field, the superconducting state is expected to exhibit a topologically non-trivial nature, as revealed by the Fermi surface of the interacting model.

Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a boundary layer devoid of free chain ends, requiring modifications to the theoretical predictions of melt brush geometry. Although the "end exclusion zone" has been successfully incorporated into models of strongly stretched brushes on the outer surfaces of cylinders and spheres, the behavior of brushes on the interfaces of spherical particles, particularly in the region near the curvature, has not been comprehensively analyzed. This study provides a quantitative expansion of the strong stretching theory to include the interface brush region of spherical particles, yielding predictions that can be tested via advanced simulation methods. By simulating the strong stretching brush near a curved interface using a precise numerical approach, we confirm that the parabolic approximation is accurate for long chains but that a significant end exclusion zone develops near the curvature, leading to a predicted melt brush geometry in equilibrium with good solvents that is approximately spherical, with a characteristic radius dependent on the ratio of chain curvature to its persistence length. This scaling applies to brushes on the interfaces of spherical particles with a wide range of curvature sizes, from very flat interfaces of block copolymer melts to brushes on the surfaces of proteins and nanoparticles.
